name: Dabinett
description: Perhaps the most widely planted and reliable English bittersweet cider apple, discovered as a seedling tree in South Petherton, Somerset in the mid-19th century. Produces medium-sized green-yellow fruit flushed with red. Renowned for yielding a high-quality, balanced bittersweet juice capable of producing exceptional single-varietal ciders or forming the structural backbone of traditional blends.
blendingGuidance: Outstanding as a single-varietal cider. In blends, it supplies soft, rounded, full-bodied bittersweet tannins without harsh bitterness, pairing well with sharp apples like Bramley or Golden Russet to elevate acidity.
pressingCharacteristics: Presses easily with good juice yields. Ferments reliably and steadily with moderate nitrogen demand, developing golden hues and pleasant mouthfeel.

name: Kingston Black
description: Revered worldwide as the 'King of Cider Apples', Kingston Black originated in Taunton, Somerset in the late 19th century. Small, dark crimson to purplish fruit. It is one of the rare heirloom varieties possessing the near-perfect natural equilibrium of malic acidity, astringent tannins, and rich sugars required to craft sublime vintage single-varietal cider without blending.
blendingGuidance: Legendary single varietal. When used in blends, adds sparkling acidity, refined phenolic structure, and complex aromatics to sweeter or duller ciders.
pressingCharacteristics: Produces deep copper-colored juice with exceptional aromatic intensity. Slow, cool fermentation is recommended to preserve delicate floral and spicy volatile compounds.

name: Yarlington Mill
description: Found growing from the masonry of a water mill at Yarlington, Somerset in 1898. Medium-sized yellow fruit with red striping. Produces beautifully smooth, mellow bittersweet ciders with distinct floral aromas and licorice/caramel undertones.
blendingGuidance: Excellent single varietal with mild acidity; blends harmoniously with sharp dessert apples or bittersharp apples to add warmth, color, and mouth-coating tannins.
pressingCharacteristics: High juice yield, presses cleanly. Generates golden, amber juice that undergoes steady primary fermentation.

name: Chisel Jersey
description: An ancient Somerset bittersweet variety producing small, firm greenish-yellow apples heavily flushed with brownish-red. Known for high specific gravity and dense, astringent tannins that impart profound structural body and rustic character.
blendingGuidance: Rarely fermented alone due to high astringency and low acidity; a prized blending component to infuse deep color, phenolic bite, and long aging potential into lighter ciders.
pressingCharacteristics: Very hard flesh that requires rigorous milling and pressing. Yields dense, tannin-rich juice with slow fermentation and low nutrient demands.

name: Foxwhelp
description: One of the oldest documented English cider apples, dating back to the early 1600s in Herefordshire and the Forest of Dean. Yellow fruit striped with deep scarlet. Celebrated for its intense, electric malic acidity combined with firm phenolic bitterness.
blendingGuidance: Used extensively as an acid-and-tannin booster in traditional English ciders. Adds brightness, crisp bite, and longevity to blends dominated by low-acid bittersweet varieties.
pressingCharacteristics: Juicy and easy to express. The striking acidity protects the must from bacterial spoilage during early fermentation.

name: Somerset Redstreak
description: A classic English bittersweet cider apple renowned for producing pleasant, fruity, and highly aromatic ciders with soft tannins and brilliant amber clarity.
blendingGuidance: Versatile blending workhorse that can be fermented as a single-varietal session cider or blended with culinary apples to supply soft phenolic texture.
pressingCharacteristics: Presses cleanly with generous yields; ferments rapidly with aromatic ester expression.

name: Tremlett's Bitter
description: Originated in the Exe Valley of Devon in the 19th century. Conical, deep red-striped fruit with hard, puckering tannins and rich aroma.
blendingGuidance: Ideal for imparting muscular astringency and drying mouthfeel to dessert fruit ciders.
pressingCharacteristics: Firm fruit that softens slightly after sweating; releases richly colored juice high in polyphenols.

name: Harry Masters Jersey
description: Selected by 19th-century cidermaker Harry Masters in Montacute, Somerset. Medium-sized, conical apple with dark red blush. Yields vintage quality bittersweet juice with baked spice and caramel nuances.
blendingGuidance: Regularly made into single varietals or combined with sharp apples to craft classic West Country dry or medium ciders.
pressingCharacteristics: High juice extraction, reliable fermentation profile, and rich golden juice that clears well.

name: Stoke Red
description: Discovered in the village of Rodney Stoke, Somerset. Small, round crimson fruit. A premier vintage bittersharp apple offering crisp malic acidity, full astringent tannins, and delicate berry aromas.
blendingGuidance: One of the few varieties capable of producing outstanding single-varietal cider alongside Kingston Black. In blends, provides vital acidity and tannin structure.
pressingCharacteristics: Very late ripening, often harvested in November or December. Juices slowly and ferments steadily in cold ambient temperatures.

name: Michelin
description: Bred in Normandy in 1872 by M. Legrand and named after pomologist Henri Michelin. Small to medium yellow-green fruit. Exceptionally popular in both France and the UK due to its reliable cropping, soft tannins, and clean, delicate apple flavor.
blendingGuidance: The quintessential cider blending workhorse. Bridges high-acid culinary apples and aggressive bittersweet varieties without overwhelming subtle flavor notes.
pressingCharacteristics: High juice yield, easy milling and pressing. Ferments cleanly with low to moderate nutrient demand.

name: Bedan
description: An ancient, highly esteemed Norman bittersweet cider apple dating back to the 16th century. Yellow-green fruit flushed with soft red. Renowned for rich, perfumed must that yields elegant, complex French Cidre with suave, velvety tannins.
blendingGuidance: Standard component in classic Norman and Breton cider blends, especially for keeving (cidre bouché) where low acidity and rich aroma are paramount.
pressingCharacteristics: Late season variety that sweats well in storage; produces golden, highly aromatic juice prone to spontaneous enzymatic clarification.

name: Binet Rouge
description: Classic Norman bittersweet variety with beautiful bright red skin and sweet, perfumed flesh. Prized throughout the Pays d'Auge for producing exceptionally aromatic and smoothly structured ciders and Calvados distillates.
blendingGuidance: Provides harmonious aromatics and mild astringency to traditional French ciders; pairs well with sharp apples to elevate balance.
pressingCharacteristics: High pressing efficiency; yields aromatic, deep rose-tinted must that ferments gently under cool conditions.

name: Médaille d'Or
description: Raised in 1884 by the Association Française Pomologique and awarded a gold medal (hence the name). Small, conical golden-yellow fruit. Famous for having one of the highest tannin concentrations of any known cider apple, alongside exceptional sugar gravity.
blendingGuidance: Never fermented as a single varietal due to overwhelming astringency and bitterness. A potent blending weapon used at 5–15% in blends to inject intense body, color, and aging potential.
pressingCharacteristics: Very late ripening, often in December. Thick, syrupy, deeply astringent juice that ferments slowly and resists oxidation.

name: Reine des Pommes
description: The 'Queen of Apples', an esteemed Breton bittersweet apple from the Ille-et-Vilaine department. Medium-sized, ribbed fruit with red-orange blush. Yields rich, full-bodied cider with pronounced rustic, farmyard, and dried fruit nuances.
blendingGuidance: Key component in authentic Breton farm ciders, bringing robust tannic backbone and rustic terroir.
pressingCharacteristics: Hard fruit that stores exceptionally well; releases copper-hued must with good natural yeast microflora.

name: Frequin Rouge
description: Traditional Norman bittersweet apple with intense crimson skin. Known for contributing deep ruby-amber color, dry phenolic grip, and rich red-fruit aromatics to Pays d'Auge ciders.
blendingGuidance: Blended with sharp and sweet varieties for balanced traditional French ciders and distillation washes for Calvados.
pressingCharacteristics: Milling and pressing are straightforward; tannins macerate rapidly upon crushing to produce richly colored juice.

name: Kermerrien
description: Originating from Finistère in Brittany. Dark red, flattened fruit. One of the few authentic French bittersharp varieties, providing crucial acidity alongside chewy tannins for Breton ciders.
blendingGuidance: Supplies crisp natural acidity and tannic structure in regions where low-acid bittersweet varieties dominate.
pressingCharacteristics: Presses easily; delivers structured, refreshing juice with distinct phenolic depth.

name: Harrison
description: The most famous American cider apple of the 18th and 19th centuries, originated in Essex County, New Jersey. Lost for decades before being rediscovered in 1976. Small yellow apple with black specks. Produces an intensely colored, rich orange cider with champagne-like brilliance, high alcohol potential, and unforgettable mouthfeel.
blendingGuidance: World-class single varietal cider apple. Blends magnificently with Hewes Crab and Golden Russet to reproduce authentic early American historic ciders.
pressingCharacteristics: High specific gravity and viscous, golden-orange juice that ferments cleanly to high alcohol while retaining body.

name: Hewes Virginia Crab
description: Documented in Virginia prior to 1700 and famously cultivated by George Washington at Mount Vernon and Thomas Jefferson at Monticello. Small, dull red crabapple. Yields a dry, aromatic, highly pungent cider packed with cinnamon, cedar, and crisp malic acid.
blendingGuidance: Ideal for single-varietal heirloom cider or as a premier acid/tannin enhancer for dessert apple bases.
pressingCharacteristics: High sugar and intense acidity prevent spoilage; yields aromatic, sparkling must that clears rapidly.

name: Golden Russet
description: Known as the 'Champagne of Cider Apples', Golden Russet originated in New York in the early 19th century. Heavily russeted, bronze-gold skin. Renowned for extremely high sugar content, dense body, crisp acidity, and rich nutty, apricot aromas.
blendingGuidance: Spectacular single varietal cider or applewine; also the ultimate sugar and flavor booster in blends.
pressingCharacteristics: Sweats into intense, sweet, syrupy juice with high original gravity; ferments reliably to 7.5–9.5% ABV.

name: Roxbury Russet
description: The oldest named American apple cultivar, discovered in Roxbury, Massachusetts in the 1630s. Large, flattened, bronze-green fruit with rough russeting. Famous for high sugar, vinous acidity, and excellent winter keeping qualities.
blendingGuidance: Produces outstanding heirloom New World ciders and blends seamlessly with bittersweet varieties to provide clean acidity and sugar.
pressingCharacteristics: High specific gravity and aromatic juice that ferments cleanly with citrus and spice character.

name: Northern Spy
description: Discovered in East Bloomfield, New York around 1800. Large, striped red-and-yellow apple celebrated for its crunchy, tender, aromatic flesh. A premier dual-purpose apple providing crisp, lively acidity and aromatic backbone in New World ciders.
blendingGuidance: The classic American cider backbone; supplies bright malic acid and clean orchard aromatics when combined with bittersweet or sweet apples.
pressingCharacteristics: High juice volume; presses cleanly and ferments rapidly into a refreshing, bright, and sparkling cider.

name: Newtown Pippin
description: Also known as Albemarle Pippin. Originated in Newtown, Queens, New York around 1730. Favored by Thomas Jefferson and Queen Victoria. Crisp, dense green apple with complex piney, citrus, and herbal flavors.
blendingGuidance: Exceptional as a single-varietal New World heritage cider, delivering crisp acidity and dry aromatic complexity.
pressingCharacteristics: Crisp flesh yielding generous juice; benefits from sweating in cold storage before milling.

name: Wickson Crab
description: Bred in Mendocino County, California by Albert Etter and named after pomologist E.J. Wickson. Small, oblong yellow-red crabapple with staggering sugar levels (up to 20° Brix) and electric, champagne-like malic acidity.
blendingGuidance: Invaluable acid and alcohol powerhouse; elevates low-acid or session cider blends with thrilling citrus-acid brightness and vinous complexity.
pressingCharacteristics: High sugar and intense acid produce potent must that ferments into crisp, wine-like ciders with natural longevity.

name: Ashmead's Kernel
description: Raised around 1700 by Dr. William Ashmead in Gloucester. Flattish russeted fruit offering an explosive burst of tart lemon acidity, pear drop, and nutty undertones.
blendingGuidance: Superb for sharp single varietals or providing crisp acid punch to English and New World cider blends.
pressingCharacteristics: Hard, dense fruit that keeps exceptionally well; yields concentrated, vinous must.

name: Gravenstein
description: An ancient heirloom variety brought to Sebastopol, California in 1811 by Russian settlers. Striped red and greenish-yellow skin. Famous for early season harvest, crisp juiciness, and intoxicating floral honey aroma.
blendingGuidance: Beloved in California and the Pacific Northwest for aromatic, fresh single-varietal summer ciders.
pressingCharacteristics: Extremely juicy; early ripening demands prompt milling and pressing to avoid mealy texture.

name: McIntosh
description: Discovered by John McIntosh in Dundela, Ontario in 1811. Vivid crimson and green skin with tender, aromatic white flesh. The defining aromatic backbone of New England and eastern Canadian craft ciders.
blendingGuidance: Brings immediate fresh apple aromatics, berry notes, and bright acidity; best blended with bittersweet or russet apples to add body and tannin.
pressingCharacteristics: Very soft fruit with high juice yield; requires gentle pressing pressure to avoid excessive pomace solids in must.

name: Granny Smith
description: Discovered in Eastwood, New South Wales by Maria Ann Smith in 1868. Bright grass-green skin with hard, juicy, tart flesh. Celebrated for pure, unadorned malic acid sharpness.
blendingGuidance: Standard acid correction apple in commercial New World ciders to sharpen bland, sweet table fruit juices.
pressingCharacteristics: Crisp and firm; mills cleanly and presses easily with crystal-clear, highly acidic juice.

name: Bramley's Seedling
description: The quintessential British culinary cooking apple, grown from seed by Mary Ann Brailsford in 1809. Large green apple with tremendous malic sharpness, crisp juice, and clean baking apple aroma.
blendingGuidance: The classic English acid-balancing apple; combined with low-acid bittersweet varieties (like Dabinett or Yarlington Mill) to achieve ideal sensory balance.
pressingCharacteristics: High acidity buffers must from spoilage; produces pale, zesty, clean-fermenting juice.

name: Golden Delicious
description: Found as a chance seedling in Clay County, West Virginia in 1890. Pale green to golden-yellow skin with sweet, mild, honeyed flavor and gentle acidity.
blendingGuidance: Acts as an inexpensive, dependable volume base in cider recipes, providing fermentable sugars and soft mouthfeel.
pressingCharacteristics: High juice yield; low acid and low tannin make it susceptible to blandness if not blended with sharp or bittersweet fruit.

name: Honeycrisp
description: Developed at the University of Minnesota in 1974. Renowned for its explosive crispness and explosive juice content, with balanced sweetness and gentle honeyed flavor.
blendingGuidance: Produces light, clean, sparkling New World ciders with fresh orchard character. Best complemented by sharp or tannic fruit.
pressingCharacteristics: Exceptionally juicy; yields large quantities of clear, pale must with low tannin astringency.

name: Thorn
description: Described in 1676 in the Three Counties of England, named after the village of Thorn in Gloucestershire. Pale yellow-green perry pear yielding exceptional single-varietal perry with exquisite elderflower aroma, crisp citrus acidity, soft astringency, and lingering unfermentable sorbitol sweetness.
blendingGuidance: One of the premier single-varietal perry pears in existence. Delivers natural sweetness from unfermentable sorbitol alongside floral elderberry and citrus brightness.
pressingCharacteristics: Narrow harvest window; fruit turns from rock hard to over-ripe rapidly. Mills smoothly and releases pale, perfumed juice that requires delicate handling to prevent oxidation.

name: Hendre Huffcap
description: Originating from Hendre Farm, Gloucestershire. Elliptical yellow fruit with slight russet. Renowned for rich, luscious mouthfeel, substantial sorbitol content, and perfumed pear aromatics.
blendingGuidance: Highly versatile in perry making; yields smooth single-varietal perry or acts as a body and sweetness enhancer in blends.
pressingCharacteristics: Good keeping quality for a perry pear; produces clear juice that settles and ferments steadily.

name: Yellow Huffcap
description: A legendary vintage perry pear renowned for potent, heady perry with high alcohol potential (the name 'Huffcap' referred to potent country ale or perry that 'lifted the cap'). Small yellow fruit with high sugars and high unfermentable sorbitol.
blendingGuidance: Produces sublime, full-bodied single-varietal perry with tropical fruit aromatics and rich, permanent residual sweetness.
pressingCharacteristics: Ripens early and rapidly; must be milled and pressed immediately upon falling to avoid rot and blackening.

name: Barland
description: Documented in 1674 in Bosbury, Herefordshire. Small green-yellow fruit. Famous for bracing, citric/malic acidity and astringent tannins that once led to its use as medicinal 'physic'. Yields a robust, long-lived perry.
blendingGuidance: Valuable acid/tannin booster in perry blends that lack crispness and definition.
pressingCharacteristics: High pectin content and prone to rapid browning; requires swift pressing and careful fining if bright clarity is desired.

name: Brandy
description: Selected in the village of Western Callow, Herefordshire. Turbinate yellow-brown fruit. Yields rich, golden-amber perry with ripe pear flesh, honeyed toffee, and lingering astringency.
blendingGuidance: Provides warm, rounded body, golden color, and pleasant bittersweet tannin structure to perry blends.
pressingCharacteristics: High sugar and moderate tannin; presses cleanly and undergoes steady fermentation.

name: Butt
description: An ancient, highly resilient perry pear from the Severn Vale. Small, turbinate green-yellow fruit. Famous for its late ripening, excellent storage keeping, and massive astringent tannins.
blendingGuidance: The standard perry blending pear for structural tannins and astringency; gives perry exceptional aging endurance.
pressingCharacteristics: Very late harvest (November). Fruit can sit in heaps without rotting; produces dense, astringent, golden juice.

name: Blakeney Red
description: Known as the 'Circus Pear' because growers could rely on its crop to pay for a trip to the circus. Heavy cropper with attractive red-flushed skin. Yields light, pleasant, easy-drinking perry.
blendingGuidance: Dependable base perry pear; produces smooth, light perry that blends easily with tannic or acidic varieties.
pressingCharacteristics: Presses cleanly and easily; juice is gentle and sweet with low tannin extraction.
